tagline: The second volume of Luke's two-part work: how the risen Jesus, by his Spirit, carried the good news from a room in Jerusalem to the capital of the Roman world.
overview:
Acts picks up where the Gospel of Luke leaves off. The risen Jesus spends forty days with his apostles, tells them to wait in Jerusalem for the Holy Spirit, and is taken up into heaven. At the Jewish festival of Pentecost the Spirit comes, Peter preaches, and about three thousand people are baptized. From there the book follows the witness outward. The first community in Jerusalem shares its goods and faces arrest and threats; Stephen becomes the first martyr; persecution scatters believers into Judea and Samaria; Philip baptizes an Ethiopian official; and Saul of Tarsus, the church's fiercest opponent, meets the risen Christ on the road to Damascus. Peter is sent to the house of a Roman centurion named Cornelius, and the Spirit falls on Gentiles (people who are not Jewish) just as it had on Jews.

The second half belongs largely to Saul, now called Paul. He and his companions travel through Cyprus, Asia Minor, Macedonia, and Greece, planting communities in cities like Philippi, Thessalonica, Corinth, and Ephesus. A council in Jerusalem (chapter 15) settles that Gentile believers need not be circumcised or keep the whole law of Moses to belong to God's people. Paul is arrested in Jerusalem, defends himself before Jewish councils, Roman governors, and a Jewish king, appeals to Caesar, survives a shipwreck, and arrives in Rome. The book closes with him under house arrest for two years, welcoming everyone who comes and proclaiming the kingdom of God without hindrance.

Acts matters because it is the only narrative we have of the church's first three decades. Without it, Paul's letters would float without a setting, and the step from a Jewish teacher executed in Judea to communities of Jews and Gentiles meeting across the empire would be almost unexplained. It is also a theological book: it insists that the church's growth is the work of the risen Christ and his Spirit, not of clever strategy, and that the gospel crosses every boundary of language, race, and class.
author:
Like the Gospels, Acts is formally anonymous, but it is plainly the second half of a work that begins with the Gospel of Luke. Both are addressed to the same man, Theophilus (Luke 1:3; Acts 1:1), and Acts opens by referring back to a first book about all that Jesus began to do and to teach. The style, vocabulary, and concerns of the two books match closely, and most scholars of every persuasion treat them as a single two-volume work, often called Luke-Acts.

From the late second century, church writers, among them Irenaeus of Lyon, name the author as Luke, a companion of Paul whom Paul's letters call a physician and fellow worker (Colossians 4:14; Philemon 24; 2 Timothy 4:11). The strongest internal evidence is the so-called we passages, stretches of the narrative where the story shifts from they to we (16:10-17; 20:5-21:18; 27:1-28:16), which read most naturally as the writer's own presence on those voyages. Many scholars accept Luke as the author on this basis. Others think the we passages come from a travel source the author used, or are a literary device, and they point to differences between Acts and Paul's own letters as reasons to doubt that a close companion wrote it. The traditional view remains widely held and has strong support.
date:
Acts ends with Paul in Rome awaiting trial, about AD 60 to 62, and there are two main positions on when it was written. The first dates it to the early 60s, soon after that point. Its defenders note that the book never mentions Paul's death, the persecution under Nero in AD 64, the martyrdom of James the Lord's brother in AD 62, or the destruction of the temple in AD 70, all events it would have had reason to report, and they read the open ending as simply where events stood when Luke wrote.

The second, held by many modern scholars, dates it to the 70s or 80s. Its defenders argue that Luke's Gospel draws on Mark, often dated to the late 60s, that Luke 21:20 (armies surrounding Jerusalem) reflects knowledge of the Roman siege, and that the open ending is a deliberate literary choice: Luke's point is that the gospel reached Rome, not what became of Paul. A smaller group of scholars, such as Richard Pervo, argue for the early second century. The book's meaning does not depend on settling the question, but the earlier date would make Acts nearly contemporary with the events of its last chapters.
setting:
Acts covers roughly three decades, from the resurrection and Pentecost (about AD 30 or 33) to Paul's house arrest in Rome (about AD 60 to 62). The whole Mediterranean world was under Roman rule. Emperors from Tiberius to Nero reigned in Rome, while Judea was governed by Roman prefects and procurators, briefly by the Jewish king Herod Agrippa I (AD 41 to 44, whose death Acts 12 describes), and then by procurators again, including Felix and Festus, before whom Paul stood trial.

Jews lived not only in Judea but in communities across the empire (the Diaspora, or dispersion), with synagogues in most cities of any size. Around those synagogues gathered Gentiles who admired Israel's God without fully converting, often called God-fearers, and they are among the first Gentiles to believe in Acts. Greek was the common language of the eastern empire, Roman roads and sea lanes made travel possible, and Roman citizenship, which Paul held, carried legal protections that matter at several points in the story. The book moves through the religious world of the empire as well: the Jerusalem temple and its priestly leadership, the Pharisees and Sadducees, local cults like that of Artemis at Ephesus, magicians, philosophers at Athens, and the imperial courts.
purpose:
Luke tells Theophilus at the start of his Gospel that he writes so that his reader may know the certainty of the things he has been taught (Luke 1:4), and Acts continues that aim. It shows that the church's message rests on public events and on witnesses, and it explains how a movement that began among Jews came to include Gentiles without requiring them to become Jews. It defends the legitimacy of that inclusion as the fulfillment of Israel's Scriptures and the plain work of God, not a betrayal of Israel.

Acts also answers questions a Roman reader might ask. Again and again Roman officials find no crime in Paul or the believers, which suggests that the movement is not a political threat to Rome. And it offers the church a model: a people who pray, share their goods, bear witness under pressure, settle disputes openly, and keep crossing boundaries at the Spirit's leading. Scholars debate how much weight each of these aims carries, but all of them are visible in the text.
story: Acts is the hinge between the Gospels and the letters. The Gospels end with Jesus risen and the command to make disciples of all nations; Acts shows that command being carried out, and it gives the setting for most of Paul's letters, which were written during the travels it describes. It also looks back across the whole Old Testament. God promised Abraham that all the families of the earth would be blessed through him, and Isaiah spoke of Israel as a light to the nations. Acts presents the church as the place where those promises begin to be fulfilled. The Spirit poured out at Pentecost answers Joel's prophecy, and the confusion of languages at Babel is met by a gift in which many languages declare the works of God. The book ends not with a conclusion but with the gospel spreading, which leaves room for the rest of church history and for the final hope of Christ's return that the angels announce in chapter 1.
christ: Acts is sometimes called the Acts of the Apostles, but its first verse suggests a better title. Luke says his first book was about all that Jesus began to do and to teach, which implies that Acts is about what Jesus continues to do, now from heaven, through his Spirit and his people. The risen Christ appears, speaks, and acts throughout: he pours out the Spirit (2:33), stands at God's right hand as Stephen dies (7:56), confronts Saul on the Damascus road (9:5), and speaks to Paul in visions (18:9; 23:11). The apostles' preaching centers on his death, his resurrection as the vindication of God, his exaltation as Lord and Christ, and the forgiveness of sins offered in his name. Acts is the church's earliest narrative account of the conviction that Jesus is alive and reigning, and that his reign is advancing through witness rather than force.
reading:
Acts is historical narrative written by an ancient historian, and it follows the conventions of ancient history writing: speeches, summaries, selected episodes, and a clear theological point of view. Read it for its large movement, from Jerusalem outward, and notice the summary statements that mark stages of growth (for example 6:7; 9:31; 12:24; 16:5; 19:20).

The most common misreading treats every event in Acts as a rule for every church. Acts describes a unique period, the founding of the church, and some of what happens (the sound of wind at Pentecost, the lot cast for Matthias) is not presented as repeatable. At the same time the book clearly intends to shape its readers. Christians differ on how much of its pattern is normative, especially on the order of faith, baptism, and receiving the Spirit, and on whether speaking in tongues is a regular sign of the Spirit's coming. A careful reader asks of each episode what Luke himself signals is typical and what is exceptional, and reads Acts alongside the teaching of the letters.

The question of historical reliability has been debated for two centuries. In the nineteenth century the Tübingen school, led by F. C. Baur, argued that Acts smooths over real conflict between Peter and Paul, and some scholars still point to tensions between Acts and Paul's letters, for example in the number and purpose of Paul's visits to Jerusalem. Others, from William Ramsay to Colin Hemer in The Book of Acts in the Setting of Hellenistic History (1989), have stressed how often Luke gets local details right. An inscription from Delphi dates Gallio's term as proconsul of Achaia to about AD 51 to 52, matching Acts 18:12; Luke correctly calls Sergius Paulus the proconsul of Cyprus (13:7); and he uses the unusual title politarchs for the city officials of Thessalonica (17:6), a title confirmed by inscriptions from that city. Both sides agree that Luke shaped his material; they differ on how freely.

structure.title: Waiting and Pentecost
structure.summary: The risen Jesus commissions his apostles and ascends. Matthias replaces Judas, and the Spirit comes at Pentecost, followed by Peter's sermon and the birth of the Jerusalem church.

structure.title: Witness in Jerusalem
structure.summary: Healing, preaching, arrest, and growth in the city. The church shares its goods, faces discipline and internal tension, and appoints seven to serve. Stephen's speech and death close the Jerusalem section.

structure.title: Judea, Samaria, and the door to the nations
structure.summary: Persecution scatters the church. Philip preaches in Samaria and to an Ethiopian, Saul is converted, Peter is sent to Cornelius, a mixed church forms at Antioch, and Herod Agrippa I opposes the apostles and dies.

structure.title: The first mission and the Jerusalem council
structure.summary: Antioch sends Barnabas and Saul through Cyprus and southern Asia Minor. The church in Jerusalem decides that Gentile believers need not be circumcised.

structure.title: Paul's missions around the Aegean
structure.summary: Paul travels through Macedonia and Greece and spends about three years in Ephesus, planting churches, facing riots, and finally setting his face toward Jerusalem.

structure.title: Paul on trial and the road to Rome
structure.summary: Paul is arrested in the temple, defends himself before crowds, councils, governors, and King Agrippa II, appeals to Caesar, survives a shipwreck, and preaches in Rome under house arrest.

themes.title: The Holy Spirit
themes.body: The Spirit is the driving force of Acts. Jesus promises the Spirit's power for witness (1:8), the Spirit comes at Pentecost, fills believers for bold speech, guides decisions, sets apart missionaries, and falls on Samaritans and Gentiles in ways that force the church to recognize them as full members. Luke uses several expressions for the Spirit's work (baptized with, filled with, poured out, received), and Christian traditions read these differently, but all agree that in Acts the church lives and moves by the Spirit rather than by its own resources.

themes.title: Witness
themes.body: The key word of the book's program is witness (1:8). The apostles are first of all witnesses of the resurrection, people who saw the risen Jesus and testify to it. Others then bear witness to what they have come to believe, often before hostile courts. The Greek word for witness later came to mean martyr, and in Acts the two ideas already touch: Stephen's witness costs him his life.

themes.title: The gospel crosses boundaries
themes.body: Acts traces the good news across line after line: from Jews in Jerusalem to Greek-speaking Jews, to Samaritans, to a eunuch from Ethiopia, to a Roman centurion, to pagans in Lystra and philosophers in Athens. Each crossing is contested, and the church often has to be pushed by God to accept it. The Jerusalem council in chapter 15 settles the central question: Gentiles are saved by grace through faith, as Jews are, without first becoming Jews.

themes.title: Continuity with Israel
themes.body: Acts insists that faith in Jesus fulfills Israel's hope rather than replacing it. The first believers are Jews who worship in the temple; the apostles preach from the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms; and Paul, even on trial, says he stands accused because of the hope of Israel. The book is honest that many of Paul's fellow Jews rejected his message, and it ends with that tension unresolved, but it never presents the church as a new religion cut loose from Israel's God.

themes.title: Suffering and the sovereignty of God
themes.body: Almost every advance in Acts comes through opposition: arrests, beatings, stonings, riots, and a shipwreck. Luke presents none of this as defeat. Persecution scatters the church and so spreads the word; Paul's imprisonment carries him to Rome at the empire's expense. God's purpose stands behind events without making the suffering less real.

keyChapters.why: The risen Jesus gives the program of the book (1:8) and ascends, with the promise that he will return.
The Spirit comes at Pentecost, and Peter's sermon sets out the first public proclamation of the risen Christ.
Stephen's long speech retells Israel's history and his death marks the end of the Jerusalem period and introduces Saul.
Saul, the persecutor, meets the risen Jesus on the road to Damascus and becomes the apostle to the Gentiles.
Peter's visit to Cornelius opens the door to the Gentiles, with the Spirit falling on them as on the first believers.
The Jerusalem council decides that Gentile believers are saved by grace without circumcision, a turning point for the whole church.
Paul's speech in Athens shows how the gospel addresses a pagan audience with no knowledge of Israel's Scriptures.
Paul reaches Rome, and the book ends with the kingdom proclaimed boldly and without hindrance at the empire's heart.
